refs.html: Shai Danziger, Jonathan Levav, Liora Avnaim-Pesso (2011). Extraneous factors in judicial decisions. PNAS 108(17):6889-6892. link
refs.authors: Shai Danziger, Jonathan Levav, Liora Avnaim-Pesso
refs.title: Extraneous factors in judicial decisions
refs.finding: Share of favorable rulings fell from about 65% to nearly 0% within each session and jumped back to about 65% after a food break. The authors read this as extraneous factors swaying rulings, but did not measure mood or hunger and could not separate rest from food.
refs.factor: Time of day / meal breaks / decision fatigue (extraneous)
refs.status: Heavily contested. Authors' reply (Danziger et al. 2011, PNAS 108:E834, 'Extraneous factors in judicial decisions persist') kept the claim after added controls. Critiques: Weinshall-Margel & Shapard 2011 (case order not random; unrepresented prisoners heard last; 3-member panels); Glockner 2016 (simulation: rational scheduling plus censoring reproduces much of the effect); Lakens 2017 blog 'Impossibly hungry judges' (effect size about d=2, odds ratio about 35, implausibly large); Daljord et al. 2019 (data refute the status-quo depletion theory); Chatziathanasiou 2022. No replication with exogenous case order found.

refs.html: Keren Weinshall-Margel, John Shapard (2011). Overlooked factors in the analysis of parole decisions. PNAS 108(42):E833 (letter). link
refs.authors: Keren Weinshall-Margel, John Shapard
refs.title: Overlooked factors in the analysis of parole decisions
refs.finding: Case ordering is not random. Unrepresented prisoners tend to be heard last in a session and succeed far less often. The original data lacked in-prison behaviour and representation status, and decisions are made by a 3-member panel (judge, criminologist, social worker). The post-break peak is therefore probably an artifact of case order, not of meals.
refs.factor: Case-order confound in the hungry-judge study
refs.status: Main published critique; original authors replied (PNAS 108:E834) that the effect persists.

refs.html: Andreas Glockner (2016). The irrational hungry judge effect revisited: Simulations reveal that the magnitude of the effect is overestimated. Judgment and Decision Making 11(6):601-610. link
refs.authors: Andreas Glockner
refs.title: The irrational hungry judge effect revisited: Simulations reveal that the magnitude of the effect is overestimated
refs.finding: Favorable rulings take longer. A minimally forward-planning rational judge who ends sessions rather than starting likely-long cases produces a drop of similar size. One methodological detail of the original analysis (session censoring) inflates the artifact even without foresight. Conclusion: the original analyses are not conclusive evidence of extraneous influence.
refs.factor: Decision fatigue / scheduling artifact
refs.status: Peer-reviewed critique; widely cited alongside Lakens 2017.

refs.html: Oystein Daljord, Oleg Urminsky, Jose-Manuel Ureta (2019). A Test of the Status Quo Theory of Depletion: Evidence from the Israeli Parole Decisions. Working paper, University of Chicago Booth (version Aug 22, 2019). link
refs.authors: Oystein Daljord, Oleg Urminsky, Jose-Manuel Ureta
refs.title: A Test of the Status Quo Theory of Depletion: Evidence from the Israeli Parole Decisions
refs.venue: Working paper, University of Chicago Booth (version Aug 22, 2019)
refs.finding: The original results 'strongly refute' the status-quo theory of depletion (tired judges default to denial). Evidence is more mixed when judge-specific depletion processes are allowed, but overall there is little support for the status-quo theory. The declines may fit a more general fatigue theory.
refs.factor: Decision fatigue (status-quo / depletion mechanism)
refs.status: Working paper; peer-reviewed publication not confirmed.

refs.html: Konstantin Chatziathanasiou (2022). Beware the Lure of Narratives: 'Hungry Judges' Should Not Motivate the Use of 'Artificial Intelligence' in Law. German Law Journal 23(4):452-464. link
refs.authors: Konstantin Chatziathanasiou
refs.title: Beware the Lure of Narratives: 'Hungry Judges' Should Not Motivate the Use of 'Artificial Intelligence' in Law
refs.finding: The hungry-judge study has 'entered common wisdom' and is cited uncritically, especially as an argument for AI adjudication, despite serious problems. Warns against accepting social-science evidence that fits preferred narratives.
refs.factor: Meta-scientific critique of the hungry-judge narrative

refs.html: Ravi Shroff, Konstantinos Vamvourellis (2022). Pretrial release judgments and decision fatigue. Judgment and Decision Making 17(6):1176-1207. link
refs.authors: Ravi Shroff, Konstantinos Vamvourellis
refs.title: Pretrial release judgments and decision fatigue
refs.finding: Release rates fall modestly in the hours before lunch and dinner, robust to covariates. No time-in-session effect otherwise, and no rebound after meal breaks. Judges' agreement with prosecutors' bail requests is unaffected by time or breaks. Any decision-fatigue effect is small and inconsistent with depletion explanations.
refs.factor: Time of day, meal breaks, decision fatigue
refs.status: Largest independent re-test; partly null, against the depletion mechanism.

refs.html: Sultan Mehmood, Avner Seror, Daniel L. Chen (2023). Ramadan fasting increases leniency in judges from Pakistan and India. Nature Human Behaviour 7:874-880. link
refs.authors: Sultan Mehmood, Avner Seror, Daniel L. Chen
refs.title: Ramadan fasting increases leniency in judges from Pakistan and India
refs.finding: More intense Ramadan fasting raises Muslim judges' acquittal rates and lowers appeal and reversal rates, without more recidivism or out-group bias. The direction is the opposite of the hungry-judge prediction.
refs.factor: Physiological deprivation / fasting (meal-related)

refs.html: Daniel L. Chen, Tobias J. Moskowitz, Kelly Shue (2016). Decision Making Under the Gambler's Fallacy: Evidence from Asylum Judges, Loan Officers, and Baseball Umpires. Quarterly Journal of Economics 131(3):1181-1242. link
refs.authors: Daniel L. Chen, Tobias J. Moskowitz, Kelly Shue
refs.title: Decision Making Under the Gambler's Fallacy: Evidence from Asylum Judges, Loan Officers, and Baseball Umpires
refs.finding: Decisions are negatively autocorrelated, independent of case merits. Asylum judges are up to about 3.3 percentage points more likely to deny if they granted the previous case. Effects are stronger for moderate and less experienced judges, after streaks, when consecutive cases are similar or close in time, and with weaker accuracy incentives. Quotas, learning and fairness preferences fit worse. Sequential contrast effects cannot be fully ruled out.
refs.factor: Sequence effects / gambler's fallacy
refs.status: Top-journal, widely cited; no failed replication found in this sweep. Effect is modest, unlike the hungry-judge effect.

refs.html: Adi Leibovitch (2016). Relative Judgments. Journal of Legal Studies 45(2):281-. link
refs.authors: Adi Leibovitch
refs.title: Relative Judgments
refs.finding: Judges judge each case against their own docket. Judges given milder caseloads impose longer sentences and more often use aggravated ranges or upward departures. Judges with graver caseloads are more lenient.
refs.jurisdiction: USA sentencing data (author based in Israel)
refs.factor: Contrast effects from caseload composition
refs.status: Peer-reviewed; consistent with sequence and contrast literature.

refs.html: Birte Englich, Thomas Mussweiler, Fritz Strack (2006). Playing dice with criminal sentences: The influence of irrelevant anchors on experts' judicial decision making. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin 32:188-200. link
refs.authors: Birte Englich, Thomas Mussweiler, Fritz Strack
refs.title: Playing dice with criminal sentences: The influence of irrelevant anchors on experts' judicial decision making
refs.finding: Sentences were pulled toward even blatantly random anchors, and experience did not reduce the effect. Mechanism: selective accessibility, since high anchors raised access to incriminating arguments (Study 4). Earlier Englich & Mussweiler (2001, J. Applied Social Psychology 31:1535-1551) found trial judges given a 34-month vs 2-month prosecutor demand in a rape vignette sentenced about 28.7 vs 18.8 months.
refs.factor: Anchoring (irrelevant / random sentencing demands)
refs.status: Classic; anchoring among judges replicated in many labs (see Bystranowski 2021 meta-analysis, which also flags possible publication bias).

refs.html: Chris Guthrie, Jeffrey J. Rachlinski, Andrew J. Wistrich (2001). Inside the Judicial Mind. Cornell Law Review 86:777. link
refs.corrections: The authors, year (2001) and venue (86 Cornell L. Rev. 777, issue 4) are correct. Keep: 167 federal magistrate judges were tested on 5 illusions (anchoring, framing, hindsight, representativeness, egocentric bias). All five significantly affected the judges, who were somewhat less susceptible than laypeople to framing and representativeness. Drop or re-source the anchoring numbers ('$10M demand in a frivolous motion; $2.21M vs $808,000'): I could not see them in any source. From memory only (not checked against the text), the 2001 anchoring problem was a motion to dismiss for failing the $75,000 diversity minimum. In that version, judges who ruled on the motion awarded about $882,000 on average vs about $1,249,000 for controls (about 29% less). Those figures do not match the cited ones.
refs.authors: Chris Guthrie, Jeffrey J. Rachlinski, Andrew J. Wistrich
refs.title: Inside the Judicial Mind
refs.finding: All five illusions significantly affected judges, who were somewhat less prone than laypeople to framing and representativeness. Anchoring: in a tort case, judges shown a $10M demand (in a frivolous motion) awarded about $2.21M on average vs $808,000 for controls.
refs.factor: Anchoring, framing, hindsight, representativeness, egocentric bias
refs.status: Foundational; extended by Rachlinski, Wistrich, Guthrie 2007 ('Blinking on the Bench', 93 Cornell L. Rev. 1: 295 Florida judges on the cognitive reflection test) and later anchoring studies.

refs.html: Jeffrey J. Rachlinski, Andrew J. Wistrich, Chris Guthrie (2015). Can Judges Make Reliable Numeric Judgments? Distorted Damages and Skewed Sentences. Indiana Law Journal 90:695. link
refs.corrections: The fields are correct: 90 Ind. L.J. 695 (2015), issue 2. The abstract confirms these findings: over 600 trial judges in three countries; shorter sentences when terms were stated in months rather than years; higher compensatory awards when judges knew of a damage cap; sentences that depended on the order of cases; and a TV court-show award that moved awards. Two items are not supported by the abstract. First, the stated direction of the order effect (a serious offender got less when a minor case came first) is not in the abstract; mark it unverified. Second, the 'frivolous $75,000 jurisdictional motion, about 29% less' result appears to be the 2001 'Inside the Judicial Mind' anchoring study, not a new 2015 experiment. Attribute it to Guthrie et al. 2001, or verify it in the 2015 full text.
refs.authors: Jeffrey J. Rachlinski, Andrew J. Wistrich, Chris Guthrie
refs.title: Can Judges Make Reliable Numeric Judgments? Distorted Damages and Skewed Sentences
refs.finding: Sentences were shorter when expressed in months than in years. Damage awards rose when judges learned of a cap. Sentences depended on the order of cases (a serious offender got less when a minor case came first). An irrelevant TV court-show award moved awards. Judges ruling first on a frivolous $75,000 jurisdictional motion later awarded about 29% less (per the authors' blog post).
refs.jurisdiction: Three countries (over 600 trial judges; exact countries not confirmed in this sweep)
refs.factor: Anchoring, unit framing, order effects
refs.status: Peer-reviewed law review; consistent with the experimental literature.

refs.html: Jeffrey J. Rachlinski, Andrew J. Wistrich (2026). Anchoring's Absurd Influence on Judging. Arkansas Law Review 79:285. link
refs.authors: Jeffrey J. Rachlinski, Andrew J. Wistrich
refs.title: Anchoring's Absurd Influence on Judging
refs.finding: An obviously irrelevant numeric anchor still shifted judges' numeric judgments. The authors call anchoring 'a particularly pernicious cognitive vulnerability' for judges.
refs.factor: Anchoring (absurd / irrelevant anchors)
refs.status: Recent (2026); builds on the authors' earlier anchoring studies.

refs.html: Piotr Bystranowski, Bartosz Janik, Maciej Próchnicki, Paulina Skórska (2021). Anchoring effect in legal decision-making: A meta-analysis. Law and Human Behavior 45(1):1-23. link
refs.authors: Piotr Bystranowski, Bartosz Janik, Maciej Próchnicki, Paulina Skórska
refs.title: Anchoring effect in legal decision-making: A meta-analysis
refs.finding: Significant anchoring overall: d=0.58 (95% CI 0.44-0.73) in studies with a control group, and d=0.91 without. Most moderator tests were nonsignificant. There is preliminary evidence that anchor relevance (and possibly anchor value and expertise) moderates the effect, and criminal-context effects are somewhat weaker than civil. Some evidence of publication bias; the authors say more studies are needed before legal anchoring is considered robust. Moderator details here come from a secondary summary.
refs.factor: Anchoring (all legal numeric judgments)
refs.status: Best quantitative synthesis; it qualifies the robustness claim because of publication bias.

refs.html: Holger Spamann, Lars Klohn, Christophe Jamin, Vikramaditya Khanna, John Zhuang Liu, Pavan Mamidi, Alexander Morell, Ivan Reidel (2021). Judges in the Lab: No Precedent Effects, No Common/Civil Law Differences. Journal of Legal Analysis 13(1):110-126. link
refs.corrections: The JLA fields and main finding are correct: 13(1):110-126, 2021, eight authors as listed (Klöhn has an umlaut). The study had 299 judges from 7 countries. Document use and reasons differ by country, not by common vs civil law. The precedent effect is 'barely detectable and estimated to be less, and bounded to be not much greater than' the effects of defendant attributes and anchors. Three fixes to the 2016 add-on. (1) JLA footnote 2 says Spamann & Klöhn (2016) 'report partial results of the present study for the USA', so it is the same experiment's US arm, not independent earlier evidence. (2) The JLS 45(2):255-280 abstract says the affirmance rates 'differed by 45 percent'; it does not say 'points'. (3) The figure of 32 judges is unverified; the JLA paper reports a US n=29. The rest is confirmed by the JLS abstract: precedent had no detectable effect, and the written reasons did not mention defendant characteristics.
refs.authors: Holger Spamann, Lars Klohn, Christophe Jamin, Vikramaditya Khanna, John Zhuang Liu, Pavan Mamidi, Alexander Morell, Ivan Reidel
refs.title: Judges in the Lab: No Precedent Effects, No Common/Civil Law Differences
refs.finding: Document use and written reasons differed by country, not by common vs civil law tradition. The precedent effect was barely detectable, estimated smaller than (and bounded not much larger than) the effects of legally irrelevant defendant attributes and sentence anchors. Earlier, Spamann & Klohn (2016, J. Legal Studies 45(2):255-280) found that with 32 US federal judges, a sympathetic vs unsympathetic defendant changed affirmance by 45 points while precedent had no detectable effect, and judges' written reasons never mentioned the defendant traits.
refs.jurisdiction: Argentina, Brazil, China, France, Germany, India, USA (299 real judges)
refs.factor: Legally irrelevant defendant attributes and sentence anchors vs precedent

refs.html: Jungwook Kim, Subok Chae (2017). Anchoring Effect of the Prosecutor's Demand on Sentence: Evidence from Korean Sexual Crime Cases. KDI Journal of Economic Policy 39(3):1-18. link
refs.authors: Jungwook Kim, Subok Chae
refs.title: Anchoring Effect of the Prosecutor's Demand on Sentence: Evidence from Korean Sexual Crime Cases
refs.finding: Judges' sentences track prosecutors' demands, more so at higher severity. A 1-month higher demand raises the sentence by about 0.25 months at the lowest quantile and about 0.78 months at the highest. The authors call for clearer sentencing guidelines.
refs.factor: Anchoring on prosecutor's sentencing demand (구형)
refs.status: Observational. The demand may carry case information, so rational updating and anchoring are not separated.

refs.html: 綿村英一郎 (Eiichiro Watamura), 分部利紘 (Toshihiro Wakebe), 佐伯昌彦 (Masahiko Saeki) (2014). 量刑分布グラフによるアンカリング効果についての実験的検証 (Experimental verification of the anchoring effect of sentencing distribution graphs). 社会心理学研究 (Japanese Journal of Social Psychology) 30(1):11-20. link
refs.authors: 綿村英一郎 (Eiichiro Watamura), 分部利紘 (Toshihiro Wakebe), 佐伯昌彦 (Masahiko Saeki)
refs.title: 量刑分布グラフによるアンカリング効果についての実験的検証 (Experimental verification of the anchoring effect of sentencing distribution graphs)
refs.venue: 社会心理学研究 (Japanese Journal of Social Psychology) 30(1):11-20
refs.finding: Participants shown a histogram with a peak at a relatively short term chose significantly shorter prison terms. A graph peak moved sentences more than a table with identical data, so the effect is attributed to the visual salience of the peak. A related KAKEN project summary (26885019) reports that lay judges' sentences followed the graph's mode and aligned with prosecutors' requests.
refs.factor: Anchoring on sentencing reference histograms (saiban-in system)
refs.status: Student sample. Field relevance is suggested but rests on a project summary only.

refs.html: Yun-chien Chang, Kong-Pin Chen, Jen-Che Liao, Chang-Ching Lin (2023). Ask more, awarded more: Evidence from Taiwan's courts. International Review of Law and Economics 76: 106171. link
refs.authors: Yun-chien Chang, Kong-Pin Chen, Jen-Che Liao, Chang-Ching Lin
refs.title: Ask more, awarded more: Evidence from Taiwan's courts
refs.venue: International Review of Law and Economics 76: 106171
refs.finding: A plaintiff's claim raises the judge's award even when the claim is not backed by market evidence. Release of public price information weakens the effect. A related trespass paper by K.-P. Chen, Y.-C. Chang and C.-C. Lin ('Anchoring Effect in Real Litigation', workshop versions 2013/2016) reported that claims and counter-claims moved less-experienced judges but not more-experienced ones (experience as a debiaser).
refs.factor: Anchoring on plaintiff's claim (civil)
refs.status: Peer-reviewed field evidence from Taiwan; the trespass paper's journal publication not confirmed.

refs.html: 馬躍中, 戴伸峰, 許華孚, 伍開遠, 許家源 (2019). 刑事案件具體求刑與量刑之比較研究 (The Comparative Research of Specific Sentencing Requests and Sentencing in Criminal Cases). 刑事政策與犯罪防治研究專刊 第23期, pp.41-61 (法務部司法官學院犯罪防治研究中心). link
refs.authors: 馬躍中, 戴伸峰, 許華孚, 伍開遠, 許家源
refs.title: 刑事案件具體求刑與量刑之比較研究 (The Comparative Research of Specific Sentencing Requests and Sentencing in Criminal Cases)
refs.venue: 刑事政策與犯罪防治研究專刊 第23期, pp.41-61 (法務部司法官學院犯罪防治研究中心)
refs.finding: Judges' prison terms average roughly 10% below the prosecutor's request. The authors found no Japanese-style '七掛・八掛' (70-80%) discount. Confession and remorse lower requests, while a principal role among co-perpetrators raises them. Surrender (自首) is associated with about 42 months shorter sentences. Context: the Control Yuan's 2012 corrective action said specific requests prejudge guilt and diverge from sentences.
refs.factor: Prosecutor's specific sentencing request (具體求刑) vs judge's sentence
refs.status: Government-institute monograph; not designed as a causal anchoring test.

refs.html: 林喜芬 (Lin Xifen), 李铮 (Li Zheng) (2026). 强制性抑或确定性：量刑建议的预决效应与发生机理——基于醉酒型危险驾驶案件的实证考察. 浙江大学学报（人文社会科学版）56(3). link
refs.authors: 林喜芬 (Lin Xifen), 李铮 (Li Zheng)
refs.title: 强制性抑或确定性：量刑建议的预决效应与发生机理——基于醉酒型危险驾驶案件的实证考察
refs.venue: 浙江大学学报（人文社会科学版）56(3)
refs.finding: Adoption of recommendations was 98-100% before and after the 2018 rule, so legal compulsion did not raise adoption. The specificity of recommendations mattered: general-type recommendations led to lighter sentences than range-type (2014-16), and range-type to heavier sentences than fixed-type (2018-20). The authors attribute the pre-determining effect to prosecutor-court consensus ('prosecutorial adjudication').
refs.factor: Procuratorate sentencing recommendations (量刑建议) as anchors / pre-determination
refs.status: Very recent (2026); single city and offense.

refs.html: Anthony Heyes, Soodeh Saberian (2019). Temperature and Decisions: Evidence from 207,000 Court Cases. American Economic Journal: Applied Economics 11(2): 238–265. link
refs.authors: Anthony Heyes, Soodeh Saberian
refs.title: Temperature and Decisions: Evidence from 207,000 Court Cases
refs.finding: A 10°F rise reduced decisions favourable to applicants by 6.55%.
refs.factor: Outdoor temperature
refs.status: Challenged: Spamann 2022 finds coding/data errors and sample selection; the extended sample reverses the sign

refs.html: Holger Spamann (2022). Comment on 'Temperature and Decisions: Evidence from 207,000 Court Cases'. American Economic Journal: Applied Economics 14(4): 519–528. link
refs.authors: Holger Spamann
refs.title: Comment on 'Temperature and Decisions: Evidence from 207,000 Court Cases'
refs.finding: Errors included weather mismatched to place and time, omitted 2001 data, and non-decision completions. Correcting them cuts the estimate by two-thirds, with a 95% CI straddling zero. Extending to 1990-2019 flips the sign and rules out the original magnitude with high confidence. No temperature or weather effect appears in US federal criminal sentencing 1992-2003.
refs.factor: Temperature/weather (replication)
refs.status: Published comment. The original authors dispute it, but the effect is fragile at best.

refs.html: Sally Evans, Peter Siminski (2020). The Effect of Outside Temperature on Criminal Court Sentencing Decisions. IZA Discussion Paper 13010. link
refs.authors: Sally Evans, Peter Siminski
refs.title: The Effect of Outside Temperature on Criminal Court Sentencing Decisions
refs.finding: Most estimates are precise zeros. Criminal court outcomes are not affected by temperature fluctuations ('unsurprising but reassuring').
refs.factor: Temperature

refs.html: Yue Hou, Peichun Wang (2020). Unpolluted decisions: Air quality and judicial outcomes in China. Economics Letters 194:109369. link
refs.corrections: The Hou & Wang citation is correct as given: Economics Letters 194:109369 (Sept 2020). It uses drug-offense decisions from 5 major Chinese cities, 2014-2015, and finds 'no more than 2%' of SD per 1 SD PM2.5 change 'with over 95% probability'. Correct the related Kahn & Li note: '9.7M cases (2014-2016), 135,924 judges' applies only to NBER w25594 (Feb 2019). The ERL version (15(8):084003, 2020) reports 157,378 judges and over 13 million cases (2014-2017), with a 1% rise in PM2.5 associated with a 0.182% increase in case handling time. Both versions concern productivity/speed, not severity.
refs.authors: Yue Hou, Peichun Wang
refs.title: Unpolluted decisions: Air quality and judicial outcomes in China
refs.finding: No meaningful effect. A 1 SD rise in PM2.5 changes sentence length by at most about 2% of its SD (over 95% probability). Related: Kahn & Li (NBER w25594, 2019; Environmental Research Letters 15:084003, 2020), with 9.7M cases and 135,924 Chinese judges, found pollution slows case disposition (lower productivity), which concerns speed rather than severity.
refs.factor: Air pollution (PM2.5) and temperature
refs.status: Peer-reviewed null for an East Asian court.

refs.html: Luis Sarmiento, Adam Nowakowski (2023). Court Decisions and Air Pollution: Evidence from Ten Million Penal Cases in India. Environmental and Resource Economics 86(3):605-644. link
refs.authors: Luis Sarmiento, Adam Nowakowski
refs.title: Court Decisions and Air Pollution: Evidence from Ten Million Penal Cases in India
refs.finding: Higher pollution exposure leads to more convictions. Back-of-the-envelope: a 1 SD drop in average pollution would mean up to 145,000 fewer convictions among active cases. Mechanism proposed: effects on judges' cognition and empathy.
refs.factor: Air pollution
refs.status: Peer-reviewed; conflicts with the Hou & Wang null for China, possibly due to institutional differences; no independent replication found.

refs.html: Ozkan Eren, Naci Mocan (2018). Emotional Judges and Unlucky Juveniles. American Economic Journal: Applied Economics 10(3): 171–205. link
refs.authors: Ozkan Eren, Naci Mocan
refs.title: Emotional Judges and Unlucky Juveniles
refs.finding: Unexpected losses lengthen juvenile dispositions in the following week (about 35 days on a 513-day mean). Expected losses and wins have no effect. The effect is larger for judges who are LSU alumni and is borne mainly by Black defendants. The week-long persistence is argued to rule out decision fatigue.
refs.factor: Mood shocks from sports results (unexpected LSU football losses)
refs.status: Replication data posted on openICPSR; no published replication or formal critique found in this sweep.

refs.html: Daniel L. Chen, Markus Loecher (2025). Mood and the malleability of moral reasoning: the impact of irrelevant factors on judicial decisions. Journal of Behavioral and Experimental Economics 116:102364. link
refs.corrections: Bibliographic fields are correct: JBEE 116:102364 (2025), DOI 10.1016/j.socec.2025.102364. Corrected finding per the published abstract: after a home-city NFL win (vs loss), immigration judges grant an additional 1.4 percentage points of asylum petitions, and bad weather has the opposite effect of a team win. Unrepresented parties bear the brunt of the NFL effects. US district judges assign 0.6 percentage points FEWER prison sentences (incidence, not 0.6% length) and 5% LONGER probation sentences after a win. The district-judge effect appears only for judges born in the same state as their current state of residence. The claim that the 2016 WP found no district-court effect was not verified. An earlier draft (Sept 2019, per Semantic Scholar) worded it as '0.6% longer prison sentences and 5% shorter probation' on the day after a loss.
refs.authors: Daniel L. Chen, Markus Loecher
refs.title: Mood and the malleability of moral reasoning: the impact of irrelevant factors on judicial decisions
refs.venue: Journal of Behavioral and Experimental Economics 116:102364
refs.finding: Immigration judges grant about 1.4-1.5 percentage points more asylum petitions the day after a home NFL win vs a loss, and bad weather acts like a loss. Effects are concentrated among unrepresented applicants. Sentencing results changed across versions: the 2016 WP found no district-court effect, while the later version reports 0.6% longer prison and 5% shorter probation after losses, only for judges born in their current state.
refs.factor: Mood (NFL results, weather)
refs.status: Published 2025. Results shifted across versions (sign convention, sample, and the sentencing effect appears only in a subgroup), which signals specification sensitivity.

refs.html: Daniel L. Chen, Arnaud Philippe (2023). Clash of norms: judicial leniency on defendant birthdays. Journal of Economic Behavior & Organization 211:324-344. link
refs.authors: Daniel L. Chen, Arnaud Philippe
refs.title: Clash of norms: judicial leniency on defendant birthdays
refs.finding: French sentences are about 1% less likely to be imposed and about 5% shorter on the defendant's birthday. US federal judges round sentence days down, except when rounding up unlocks good-behavior credits. No effect on days just before or after. The 2018 WP reported different magnitudes (e.g., 3% shorter in France, 15% in New Orleans) and a larger effect when judge and defendant share race.
refs.factor: Defendant's birthday (social-norm / reference-dependent leniency)
refs.status: Peer-reviewed. Magnitudes changed between WP and journal; no independent replication found.

refs.html: Kyoungmin Cho, Christopher M. Barnes, Cristiano L. Guanara (2017). Sleepy Punishers Are Harsh Punishers: Daylight Saving Time and Legal Sentences. Psychological Science 28(2). link
refs.authors: Kyoungmin Cho, Christopher M. Barnes, Cristiano L. Guanara
refs.title: Sleepy Punishers Are Harsh Punishers: Daylight Saving Time and Legal Sentences
refs.finding: Sentences on 'sleepy Mondays' were about 5% longer.
refs.factor: Sleep loss (DST transition)
refs.status: Failed re-analysis: Spamann 2018 found the reported model differed from the one described, the described model is nonsignificant, and 2004-2016 data show no effect (even shorter sentences).

refs.html: Holger Spamann (2018). Are Sleepy Punishers Really Harsh Punishers? Comment on Cho, Barnes, and Guanara (2017). Psychological Science 29(6): 1006–1009. link
refs.authors: Holger Spamann
refs.title: Are Sleepy Punishers Really Harsh Punishers? Comment on Cho, Barnes, and Guanara (2017)
refs.finding: The original significance depends on an undisclosed model, a variable transformation and sample restrictions. The described (better) model is nonsignificant. Accounting for the any-prison margin shrinks the effect to small and nonsignificant, and the opposite holds on the second harshness dimension. 2004-2016 'sleepy Mondays' show shorter and rarer sentences.
refs.factor: Sleep loss / DST (replication)
refs.status: Published comment; no rebuttal found in this sweep.

refs.html: Arnaud Philippe, Aurélie Ouss (2018). 'No Hatred or Malice, Fear or Affection': Media and Sentencing. Journal of Political Economy 126(5):2134-2178. link
refs.authors: Arnaud Philippe, Aurélie Ouss
refs.title: 'No Hatred or Malice, Fear or Affection': Media and Sentencing
refs.finding: Sentences are about 3 months longer when the verdict follows coverage of crime. The effect tracks media exposure to crime, not crime itself, and fades quickly. Professional experience and expertise appear to reduce the influence.
refs.factor: Media attention (TV crime news unrelated to the case)

refs.html: Claire S. H. Lim, James M. Snyder Jr., David Stromberg (2015). The Judge, the Politician, and the Press: Newspaper Coverage and Criminal Sentencing across Electoral Systems. American Economic Journal: Applied Economics 7(4):103-135. link
refs.corrections: Minor: the third author is spelled David Strömberg (with an umlaut). DOI 10.1257/app.20140111.
refs.authors: Claire S. H. Lim, James M. Snyder Jr., David Stromberg
refs.title: The Judge, the Politician, and the Press: Newspaper Coverage and Criminal Sentencing across Electoral Systems
refs.finding: Coverage raises sentence length for violent crimes among nonpartisan elected judges only. No effect for partisan-elected or appointed judges.
refs.factor: Media coverage x electoral accountability

refs.html: Carlos Berdejo, Noam Yuchtman (2013). Crime, Punishment, and Politics: An Analysis of Political Cycles in Criminal Sentencing. Review of Economics and Statistics 95(3):741-756. link
refs.corrections: Wording only: the 50% figure is for discretionary departures ABOVE the guidelines range (upward departures) for serious crimes in Washington State, not departures in general. DOI 10.1162/REST_a_00296. The Huber & Gordon add-on is right: AJPS 48(2):247-263 (2004), 'Accountability and Coercion: Is Justice Blind when It Runs for Office?', 22,095 Pennsylvania criminal cases from the 1990s, judges more punitive as standing for reelection approaches.
refs.authors: Carlos Berdejo, Noam Yuchtman
refs.title: Crime, Punishment, and Politics: An Analysis of Political Cycles in Criminal Sentencing
refs.finding: Sentences are about 10% longer at the end of the electoral cycle. Guideline departures are 50% more frequent and explain much of the effect. No cycle for judges not seeking re-election. Huber & Gordon (2004, AJPS) earlier found Pennsylvania judges grew more punitive as retention elections approached (22,095 cases).
refs.factor: Re-election cycles
refs.status: Replicates within the original states but generalizes poorly (Dippel & Poyker 2021).

refs.html: Christian Dippel, Michael Poyker (2021). Rules versus norms: How formal and informal institutions shape judicial sentencing cycles. Journal of Comparative Economics 49(3):645-659 (NBER w25716 earlier). link
refs.corrections: The citation fields are correct: Dippel & Poyker, J. Comparative Economics 49(3):645-659, 2021, DOI 10.1016/j.jce.2021.02.003. The earlier NBER WP is w25716, titled 'How Common are Electoral Cycles in Criminal Sentencing?' (Mar 2019, rev. Sep 2020). Corrected finding: earlier studies drew on only four states (PA, WA, NC, KS). With data on seven more states, the authors find large, previously unnoted differences in sentencing cycles across states. The working paper confirms cycles in PA, WA AND North Carolina, not only PA and WA. It finds little evidence of cycles in any newly added state: GA, MN and KY are precise nulls, AL, CO and TN are inconclusive, and VA (appointed judges) is negative and insignificant. The differences track informal norms (the baseline probability that an incumbent is challenged, and donations per race), and formal electoral institutions explain them poorly. Drop the 'two-thirds', 'not publication bias' and 'site selection (early-digitizing states)' claims unless they are checked against the published full text.
refs.authors: Christian Dippel, Michael Poyker
refs.title: Rules versus norms: How formal and informal institutions shape judicial sentencing cycles
refs.venue: Journal of Comparative Economics 49(3):645-659 (NBER w25716 earlier)
refs.finding: Reproduces electoral sentencing cycles in previously studied states (PA, WA), but finds none in about two-thirds of newly added states. The variation tracks informal norms of whether incumbents get challenged, not formal institutions. Not explained by publication bias, though site selection (early-digitizing states) may explain the original findings.
refs.jurisdiction: USA (10 states incl. PA, WA and new states)
refs.factor: Re-election cycles (replication / external validity)
refs.status: Key external-validity check: an effect real in some places but not universal.

refs.html: Daniel L. Chen, Viknesh Nagarathinam (n.d. (working paper; cites 2021-22 events)). Deadlines, Judicial Decisions, and Firm Outcomes: Evidence from Productivity Quotas in Croatia. Working paper (hosted on D. L. Chen's NBER page). link
refs.corrections: Optional detail: the data are 4.1M Croatian civil and commercial suits decided 2010-2016, about 1M of them matched to defendant-firm balance sheets. The PDF has no date. Its metadata title is 'Croatia_Quotas_AERInsights_2', which suggests an AER: Insights submission. The latest works it cites are from 2021.
refs.authors: Daniel L. Chen, Viknesh Nagarathinam
refs.title: Deadlines, Judicial Decisions, and Firm Outcomes: Evidence from Productivity Quotas in Croatia
refs.venue: Working paper (hosted on D. L. Chen's NBER page)
refs.finding: Case closures surge in the final days of each month in every year, court and case type. Month-end rulings come faster after the last hearing, are about 9% more likely to be appealed, and are followed by about one-third lower defendant-firm profit. The authors argue that selection of easy cases for month-end would bias against these results.
refs.factor: End-of-period clearance deadlines / productivity quotas

refs.html: Miguel F. P. de Figueiredo, Alexandra D. Lahav, Peter Siegelman (2020). The Six-Month List and the Unintended Consequences of Judicial Accountability. Cornell Law Review 105:363. link
refs.authors: Miguel F. P. de Figueiredo, Alexandra D. Lahav, Peter Siegelman
refs.title: The Six-Month List and the Unintended Consequences of Judicial Accountability
refs.finding: Judges close substantially more cases and decide more motions in the week before the list is compiled. Average motion time falls by 10-30 days, but rises for motions least pressed by the deadline. Suggestive evidence of more errors under deadline pressure.
refs.factor: Reporting deadlines / backlog accountability

refs.html: 蔡劭偉 (Shao-Wei Tsai); advisors 林明仁, 樊家忠 (2022). 論我國地方法院判決數量與品質間之關係 (Do more verdicts lead to higher reversal rate in Taiwan's district court?). Master's thesis, Graduate Institute of Economics, National Taiwan University (DOI 10.6342/NTU202200140). link
refs.corrections: Minor: 林明仁 is the advisor and 樊家忠 (Elliott Fan) the co-advisor. The data are 2011-2020 criminal verdicts from district and high courts.
refs.authors: 蔡劭偉 (Shao-Wei Tsai); advisors 林明仁, 樊家忠
refs.title: 論我國地方法院判決數量與品質間之關係 (Do more verdicts lead to higher reversal rate in Taiwan's district court?)
refs.venue: Master's thesis, Graduate Institute of Economics, National Taiwan University (DOI 10.6342/NTU202200140)
refs.finding: Judges produce more verdicts at month-end, when Judicial Yuan monthly reports count pending cases. There is no evidence that month-end verdicts are more often appealed or reversed. After controlling for trial length, defendants whose cases close at month-end receive shorter sentences. The author suggests simpler cases are cleared then.
refs.factor: End-of-month clearance pressure (monthly reports to the Judicial Yuan)
refs.status: Unpublished thesis. Case-selection vs pressure is not fully separated.

refs.html: Christoph Engel, Keren Weinshall (2020). Manna from Heaven for Judges: Judges' Reaction to a Quasi-Random Reduction in Caseload. Journal of Empirical Legal Studies 17(4):722-751. link
refs.corrections: Optional: add DOI 10.1111/jels.12265.
refs.authors: Christoph Engel, Keren Weinshall
refs.title: Manna from Heaven for Judges: Judges' Reaction to a Quasi-Random Reduction in Caseload
refs.finding: Lower caseload per judge led judges to invest more in each case. Plaintiffs won more often, recovered a larger share of claims and were more often reimbursed for costs. Workload shapes outcomes, not just speed.
refs.factor: Caseload / workload

refs.html: 黃意婷 (Yi-Ting Huang); advisor 樊家忠 (2023). 司法或正義？法官對減刑條例的判刑變化 (Law or Justice? Judges' Responses to Commutation). Master's thesis, Department of Economics, National Taiwan University (DOI 10.6342/NTU202302555). link
refs.authors: 黃意婷 (Yi-Ting Huang); advisor 樊家忠
refs.title: 司法或正義？法官對減刑條例的判刑變化 (Law or Justice? Judges' Responses to Commutation)
refs.venue: Master's thesis, Department of Economics, National Taiwan University (DOI 10.6342/NTU202302555)
refs.finding: After the Act took effect, judges raised sentences for commutation-eligible thefts by about 43 days (+24.7%) and cut sentences for ineligible ones by about 18 days (-12.5%). Read as a compromise between proportionality and justice, with pre-commutation sentences as a reference point. Effects lasted at least 6 months and correlated with colleagues' severity in the same court (peer effects). An earlier NTU thesis (Tsai Wei-Che 2018, advisor Lin Ming-Jen) found +30-40 days (17-22%).
refs.jurisdiction: Taiwan (theft cases around the 2007 Criminal Commutation Act)
refs.factor: Reference-point anchoring / compensating behavior after a legal shock; peer effects

refs.html: Christina L. Boyd, Lee Epstein, Andrew D. Martin (2010). Untangling the Causal Effects of Sex on Judging. American Journal of Political Science 54(2): 389-411. link
refs.authors: Christina L. Boyd, Lee Epstein, Andrew D. Martin
refs.title: Untangling the Causal Effects of Sex on Judging
refs.finding: Mostly a null result: no individual or panel effect of judge sex in 12 of 13 areas of law. The one exception is sex-discrimination cases: male judges are about 10 percentage points less likely to rule for the party alleging discrimination, and men sitting with a woman on a panel become significantly more pro-plaintiff. The authors read this as support for an informational account of gendered judging.
refs.factor: Judge gender (individual effect and panel composition)
refs.status: Widely cited; won APSA lasting-contribution recognition. Shows gender effects are narrow, limited to particular case types.

refs.html: Moses Shayo, Asaf Zussman (2011). Judicial Ingroup Bias in the Shadow of Terrorism. Quarterly Journal of Economics 126(3): 1447-1484. link
refs.authors: Moses Shayo, Asaf Zussman
refs.title: Judicial Ingroup Bias in the Shadow of Terrorism
refs.finding: Robust evidence of judicial in-group bias: plaintiffs do better before a judge of their own ethnicity. The bias is strongly associated with terrorism intensity near the court in the year before the ruling, consistent with group salience increasing social identification. A secondary summary gives a magnitude of about 18 percentage points; that figure is not from the abstract.
refs.factor: Judge ethnicity / in-group bias; interaction with terrorism intensity (situational salience)
refs.status: Seminal. The authors' 2017 AEJ: Applied follow-up (seen in search summary only) reports that bias did not generally attenuate after violence fell.

refs.html: Guy Grossman, Oren Gazal-Ayal, Samuel D. Pimentel, Jeremy M. Weinstein (2016). Descriptive Representation and Judicial Outcomes in Multiethnic Societies. American Journal of Political Science 60(1): 44-69. link
refs.authors: Guy Grossman, Oren Gazal-Ayal, Samuel D. Pimentel, Jeremy M. Weinstein
refs.title: Descriptive Representation and Judicial Outcomes in Multiethnic Societies
refs.finding: Outcomes for Jewish defendants do not depend on panel ethnic composition. Arab defendants receive more lenient punishment when the panel includes at least one Arab judge: incarceration falls 14-20% and prison sentences fall 15-26%, relative to all-Jewish panels.
refs.factor: Panel ethnic composition (descriptive representation)

refs.html: Oren Gazal-Ayal, Raanan Sulitzeanu-Kenan (2010). Let My People Go: Ethnic In-Group Bias in Judicial Decisions - Evidence from a Randomized Natural Experiment. Journal of Empirical Legal Studies 7(3): 403-428. link
refs.authors: Oren Gazal-Ayal, Raanan Sulitzeanu-Kenan
refs.title: Let My People Go: Ethnic In-Group Bias in Judicial Decisions - Evidence from a Randomized Natural Experiment
refs.finding: Judges favored suspects of their own ethnic group in the decision whether to detain. Once detention was ordered, there was no ethnic bias in its length.
refs.factor: Judge-defendant ethnic match
refs.status: Peer-reviewed; frequently cited alongside Shayo & Zussman.

refs.html: Briggs Depew, Ozkan Eren, Naci Mocan (2017). Judges, Juveniles, and In-Group Bias. Journal of Law and Economics 60(2): 209-239. link
refs.authors: Briggs Depew, Ozkan Eren, Naci Mocan
refs.title: Judges, Juveniles, and In-Group Bias
refs.finding: Negative in-group bias: Black or white juveniles assigned to a judge of their own race are more likely to be placed in custody rather than on probation, and they receive longer sentences.
refs.factor: Judge-defendant race match
refs.status: Peer-reviewed. A counterexample showing that in-group effects can run in the opposite direction.

refs.html: Elliott Ash, Sam Asher, Aditi Bhowmick, Sandeep Bhupatiraju, Daniel L. Chen, Tanaya Devi, Christoph Goessmann, Paul Novosad, Bilal Siddiqi (2025). In-Group Bias in the Indian Judiciary: Evidence from 5 Million Criminal Cases. Review of Economics and Statistics (2025); earlier CGD Working Paper 637 (2023). link
refs.authors: Elliott Ash, Sam Asher, Aditi Bhowmick, Sandeep Bhupatiraju, Daniel L. Chen, Tanaya Devi, Christoph Goessmann, Paul Novosad, Bilal Siddiqi
refs.title: In-Group Bias in the Indian Judiciary: Evidence from 5 Million Criminal Cases
refs.venue: Review of Economics and Statistics (2025); earlier CGD Working Paper 637 (2023)
refs.finding: Tight zero aggregate in-group bias by gender or religion, even where identity should be salient (for example, victim and defendant of different identities). There is some in-group bias by shared rare last name (a caste proxy), but its aggregate impact is small. The working paper reports a small religious in-group effect during Ramadan.
refs.factor: Judge-defendant gender and religion match; caste proxy (shared rare surname)
refs.status: Major null result at scale; published in REStat. Abstract wording differs across versions.

refs.html: Donghyun Danny Choi, J. Andrew Harris, Fiona Shen-Bayh (2022). Ethnic Bias in Judicial Decision Making: Evidence from Criminal Appeals in Kenya. American Political Science Review 116(3): 1067-1080. link
refs.authors: Donghyun Danny Choi, J. Andrew Harris, Fiona Shen-Bayh
refs.title: Ethnic Bias in Judicial Decision Making: Evidence from Criminal Appeals in Kenya
refs.finding: Judges are 3-5 percentage points more likely to rule for a coethnic defendant. The effect is concentrated among Kikuyu judges, the largest and politically dominant group. Text analysis shows more trust sentiment toward coethnics, suggesting in-group favoritism rather than out-group derogation. The authors' blog says the bias does not appear driven by political incentives.
refs.factor: Judge-defendant coethnicity

refs.html: Cass R. Sunstein, David Schkade, Lisa Michelle Ellman (2004). Ideological Voting on Federal Courts of Appeals: A Preliminary Investigation. Virginia Law Review 90: 301. link
refs.authors: Cass R. Sunstein, David Schkade, Lisa Michelle Ellman
refs.title: Ideological Voting on Federal Courts of Appeals: A Preliminary Investigation
refs.finding: Party-of-appointment voting and panel effects (amplification by like-minded colleagues, dampening by opposite-party colleagues) appear in affirmative action, campaign finance, sex discrimination, sexual harassment, disability, environmental and other areas. Party differences are absent in criminal appeals, federalism and takings. In abortion and capital punishment, judges vote by party but there is no panel effect.
refs.factor: Political party of appointing president; panel effects (amplification and dampening)
refs.status: Foundational and much extended. Concern about the party proxy is standard.

refs.html: Alma Cohen, Crystal S. Yang (2019). Judicial Politics and Sentencing Decisions. American Economic Journal: Economic Policy 11(1): 160-191. link
refs.authors: Alma Cohen, Crystal S. Yang
refs.title: Judicial Politics and Sentencing Decisions
refs.finding: Relative to Democratic appointees, Republican-appointed judges give Black defendants 3.0 more months than similar non-Black defendants, and give female defendants 2.0 fewer months than similar males. These gaps equal 65% of the baseline racial gap and 17% of the baseline gender gap. Other judge characteristics do not explain them, and the gaps grow when judges have more discretion.
refs.factor: Judge political affiliation x defendant race and gender
refs.status: Peer-reviewed. The working paper reported 2.1 months for the gender gap.

refs.html: Adam N. Glynn, Maya Sen (2015). Identifying Judicial Empathy: Does Having Daughters Cause Judges to Rule for Women's Issues?. American Journal of Political Science 59(1): 37-54. link
refs.authors: Adam N. Glynn, Maya Sen
refs.title: Identifying Judicial Empathy: Does Having Daughters Cause Judges to Rule for Women's Issues?
refs.finding: Holding the number of children constant, judges with daughters vote in a more feminist direction on gender-related issues. The effect is driven mainly by Republican-appointed judges and appears in gender-related civil cases but not in criminal cases such as sexual assault (per press coverage).
refs.factor: Judge family composition (daughters)
refs.status: Peer-reviewed. Effect magnitudes in the press (7%, 16%) are secondary.

refs.html: Allison P. Harris, Maya Sen (2019). Bias and Judging. Annual Review of Political Science 22: 241-259. link
refs.authors: Allison P. Harris, Maya Sen
refs.title: Bias and Judging
refs.finding: Race, ethnicity and gender sometimes predict judicial decisions in limited kinds of cases, but ideology or partisanship matters far more. The authors caution that treating judges as biased simply because they rule differently is questionable.
refs.factor: Judge race, ethnicity, gender vs ideology

refs.html: Allison P. Harris, Maya Sen (2026). How Judges' Professional Experience Impacts Case Outcomes: An Examination of Public Defenders and Criminal Sentencing. Journal of Politics 88(1): 431–437 (online December 2024). link
refs.authors: Allison P. Harris, Maya Sen
refs.title: How Judges' Professional Experience Impacts Case Outcomes: An Examination of Public Defenders and Criminal Sentencing
refs.finding: Defendants assigned to former public defenders are on average less likely to be incarcerated, and sentences are sometimes shorter, partly because these judges give fewer extremely long sentences. The effect holds for both Republican and Democratic appointees. The authors estimate that raising the share of judges with public-defender experience to about one-third would mean about 13,000 fewer incarceration sentences over ten years.
refs.factor: Prior career (former public defenders)
refs.status: Peer-reviewed. Among the first causal estimates of prior professional experience, as opposed to demographics.

refs.html: David S. Abrams, Marianne Bertrand, Sendhil Mullainathan (2012). Do Judges Vary in Their Treatment of Race?. Journal of Legal Studies 41(2): 347-383. link
refs.authors: David S. Abrams, Marianne Bertrand, Sendhil Mullainathan
refs.title: Do Judges Vary in Their Treatment of Race?
refs.finding: The Black-white incarceration gap varies substantially across judges: moving from the 10th to the 90th percentile judge raises the gap by 18 percentage points (mean incarceration 51% Black, 38% white). The sentence-length variation (10 months) cannot be distinguished from no race effect. Judge gender and age do not predict the differential; there is somewhat stronger evidence of a smaller gap among Black judges. The design cannot tell which direction any individual judge's bias runs.
refs.factor: Inter-judge heterogeneity in race treatment; judge characteristics

refs.html: Jaya Ramji-Nogales, Andrew I. Schoenholtz, Philip G. Schrag (2007). Refugee Roulette: Disparities in Asylum Adjudication. Stanford Law Review 60(2): 295. link
refs.authors: Jaya Ramji-Nogales, Andrew I. Schoenholtz, Philip G. Schrag
refs.title: Refugee Roulette: Disparities in Asylum Adjudication
refs.finding: Huge disparities among adjudicators in the same office handling applicants from the same country. Colombian applicants in Miami had a 5% chance before one judge and 88% before another in the same building, and some asylum officers granted no Chinese applicants while others granted up to 68%. Judge gender and pre-appointment work experience were strongly associated with grant rates. Representation quality had a very large effect. The authors propose training, independent appellate review and professionalization, not quotas.
refs.jurisdiction: USA (asylum offices, immigration courts, BIA, courts of appeals)
refs.factor: Inter-adjudicator disparity; judge gender and prior work experience
refs.status: Landmark. In the same issue, Legomsky argues some inconsistency is unavoidable and must be weighed against the cost of eliminating it.

refs.html: James M. Anderson, Jeffrey R. Kling, Kate Stith (1999). Measuring Interjudge Sentencing Disparity: Before and After the Federal Sentencing Guidelines. Journal of Law and Economics 42(S1): 271–308. link
refs.authors: James M. Anderson, Jeffrey R. Kling, Kate Stith
refs.title: Measuring Interjudge Sentencing Disparity: Before and After the Federal Sentencing Guidelines
refs.finding: Metadata confirmed; abstract not retrieved. From prior knowledge, not re-verified here: it quantifies 'the judge lottery' as the expected sentence difference between judges and reports reduced disparity after the Guidelines.
refs.factor: Inter-judge disparity; effect of sentencing guidelines

refs.html: Crystal S. Yang (2014). Have Interjudge Sentencing Disparities Increased in an Advisory Guidelines Regime? Evidence from Booker. New York University Law Review 89: 1268. link
refs.authors: Crystal S. Yang
refs.title: Have Interjudge Sentencing Disparities Increased in an Advisory Guidelines Regime? Evidence from Booker
refs.finding: Inter-judge sentencing disparities doubled after the Guidelines became advisory. Democratic and female judges were more likely to use their new discretion, and post-Booker appointees were less anchored to the Guidelines. Prosecutors appear to apply mandatory minimums selectively depending on the assigned judge, a major additional source of disparity.
refs.factor: Inter-judge disparity under advisory vs mandatory guidelines; judge demographics; prosecutors
refs.status: Peer-reviewed law review; a 2013 Harvard Olin working paper has the same title.

refs.html: Jeffrey R. Kling (2006). Incarceration Length, Employment, and Earnings. American Economic Review 96(3):863-876. link
refs.authors: Jeffrey R. Kling
refs.title: Incarceration Length, Employment, and Earnings
refs.finding: Using randomly assigned judges as instruments, finds no consistent evidence that longer incarceration harms post-release employment or earnings (Florida state; California federal).
refs.factor: Judge harshness as instrument

refs.html: Will Dobbie, Jacob Goldin, Crystal S. Yang (2018). The Effects of Pretrial Detention on Conviction, Future Crime, and Employment: Evidence from Randomly Assigned Judges. American Economic Review 108(2):201-40. link
refs.authors: Will Dobbie, Jacob Goldin, Crystal S. Yang
refs.title: The Effects of Pretrial Detention on Conviction, Future Crime, and Employment: Evidence from Randomly Assigned Judges
refs.finding: Detention substantially increases conviction (mostly via guilty pleas), has no net effect on future crime, and reduces formal employment.
refs.factor: Bail-judge leniency
refs.status: Canonical; later re-examined by Frandsen et al. 2023

refs.html: Manudeep Bhuller, Gordon B. Dahl, Katrine V. Løken, Magne Mogstad (2020). Incarceration, Recidivism, and Employment. Journal of Political Economy 128(4): 1269-1324. link
refs.authors: Manudeep Bhuller, Gordon B. Dahl, Katrine V. Løken, Magne Mogstad
refs.title: Incarceration, Recidivism, and Employment
refs.finding: Randomly assigned Norwegian judges differ in their propensity to imprison. Imprisonment cuts five-year reoffending probability by 29 percentage points and reduces charges by 11. The effect is concentrated among the previously non-employed, who increase their participation in employment programs. For the previously employed there is no recidivism effect and a lasting negative employment effect. OLS has the wrong sign because of selection.
refs.factor: Judge stringency (inter-judge variation in imprisonment propensity)
refs.status: Peer-reviewed. A key European civil-law example of random assignment generating measurable judge heterogeneity.

refs.html: Brigham Frandsen, Lars Lefgren, Emily Leslie (2023). Judging Judge Fixed Effects. American Economic Review 113(1): 253-277. link
refs.authors: Brigham Frandsen, Lars Lefgren, Emily Leslie
refs.title: Judging Judge Fixed Effects
refs.finding: Proposes a test (E[Y|judge] should be linear in E[D|judge]) and applies it. When the assumptions fail, it offers weaker conditions under which IV still yields a proper weighted average of effects. Stata (testjfe) and R (ivcheck) implementations exist.
refs.factor: Validity of judge-leniency designs

refs.html: Henrik Sigstad (2026). Monotonicity among Judges: Evidence from Judicial Panels and Consequences for Judge IV Designs. American Economic Review 116(1): 189-208. link
refs.authors: Henrik Sigstad
refs.title: Monotonicity among Judges: Evidence from Judicial Panels and Consequences for Judge IV Designs
refs.finding: The judge strictness ordering is violated in many cases, but the resulting bias in 2SLS judge-IV estimates appears small (per BI summary). A related Bhuller & Sigstad (2022, Economics Letters) Norwegian study fails to reject average monotonicity using appeals and reversals.
refs.jurisdiction: Norway (panel votes); summary also mentions Brazil (São Paulo Appeal Court) and the US
refs.factor: Whether 'strict' judges are uniformly strict (monotonicity)
refs.status: Recent (2026). A 2026 preregistered vignette experiment with Polish prosecutors extends this.

refs.html: Daniel L. Chen, Matt Dunn, Levent Sagun, Hale Sirin (2017). Early Predictability of Asylum Court Decisions. TSE Working Paper 17-781; later in proceedings of ICAIL (ACM Int'l Conf. on AI and Law). link
refs.authors: Daniel L. Chen, Matt Dunn, Levent Sagun, Hale Sirin
refs.title: Early Predictability of Asylum Court Decisions
refs.venue: TSE Working Paper 17-781; later in proceedings of ICAIL (ACM Int'l Conf. on AI and Law)
refs.finding: Final outcomes can be predicted with 80% accuracy when the case opens, using mainly judge identity and applicant nationality. Judges vary widely in predictability; highly predictable judges (near-always grant or deny) hold fewer hearing sessions. The authors suggest snap or predetermined judgments may be at work.
refs.factor: Predictability of outcome from judge identity and applicant nationality
refs.status: Influential working paper; a French analogue study reportedly prompted France's 2019 ban (see langford2019).

refs.html: Daniel L. Chen (2019). Judicial Analytics and the Great Transformation of American Law. Artificial Intelligence and Law 27(1): 15-42. link
refs.authors: Daniel L. Chen
refs.title: Judicial Analytics and the Great Transformation of American Law
refs.finding: Argues judicial analytics can expose extra-legal influences (bias, time of day) and be used for debiasing. Proposes disparities in how predictable judges are as a fairness criterion distinct from disparities in predicted outcomes. Predictive models with exogenous features can serve as the first stage for causal inference.
refs.factor: Extra-legal influences; predictability as a fairness criterion

refs.html: Jason Tashea (2019). Loi n° 2019-222 du 23 mars 2019 de programmation 2018-2022 et de réforme pour la justice, article 33. ABA Journal (7 June 2019). link
refs.authors: Jason Tashea
refs.title: Loi n° 2019-222 du 23 mars 2019 de programmation 2018-2022 et de réforme pour la justice, article 33
refs.finding: The identity data of magistrates and court clerks may not be reused to evaluate, analyse, compare or predict their actual or presumed professional practices.
refs.factor: Ethics/legality of judge-level analytics
refs.status: In force; criticised by empirical legal scholars

refs.html: Malcolm Langford, Mikael Rask Madsen (2019). France Criminalises Research on Judges. Verfassungsblog (22 June 2019). link
refs.authors: Malcolm Langford, Mikael Rask Madsen
refs.title: France Criminalises Research on Judges
refs.finding: Calls France the first country to explicitly ban research on individual judicial behaviour. Says the ban was prompted partly by a 2016 machine-learning study of French asylum judges that found large inter-judge differences. Argues the ban is disproportionate, also covers doctrinal scholarship, violates freedom of expression and academic freedom, and is likely incompatible with EU law.
refs.factor: Academic freedom vs judge-identity analytics
refs.status: Commentary; the post page was only partly retrievable, so the argument is summarized from search results.

refs.html: J. Mark Ramseyer, Eric B. Rasmusen (1997). Judicial Independence in Civil Law Regimes: Econometrics from Japan. Journal of Law, Economics, & Organization 13: 259–286. link
refs.authors: J. Mark Ramseyer, Eric B. Rasmusen
refs.title: Judicial Independence in Civil Law Regimes: Econometrics from Japan
refs.finding: The career system rewards able and productive judges. There is no evidence of lasting school cliques or of favoring mediators over adjudicators. Judges who joined a leftist group in the 1960s still had worse posts in the 1980s, judges who often ruled against the government early on lagged their peers, and each anti-government ruling raised the risk of transfer to a less attractive post.
refs.factor: Career incentives in a career judiciary; elite school cliques; political rulings

refs.html: J. Mark Ramseyer, Eric B. Rasmusen (2001). Why Are Japanese Judges So Conservative in Politically Charged Cases?. American Political Science Review 95(2): 331-344. link
refs.authors: J. Mark Ramseyer, Eric B. Rasmusen
refs.title: Why Are Japanese Judges So Conservative in Politically Charged Cases?
refs.finding: Judges who deferred to the ruling LDP in politically salient disputes got better posts. Judges who enjoined the national government got worse ones, and judges in a leftist group were promoted more slowly. The authors attribute the lack of heterodox rulings to the career structure.
refs.factor: Career and promotion incentives; political deference
refs.status: Expanded in the authors' 2003 book 'Measuring Judicial Independence' (U. Chicago Press). Challenged by fukumoto2015.

refs.html: Kentaro Fukumoto, Mikitaka Masuyama (2015). Measuring Judicial Independence Reconsidered: Survival Analysis, Matching, and Average Treatment Effects. Japanese Journal of Political Science. link
refs.authors: Kentaro Fukumoto, Mikitaka Masuyama
refs.title: Measuring Judicial Independence Reconsidered: Survival Analysis, Matching, and Average Treatment Effects
refs.finding: Critique: Ramseyer and Rasmusen mishandled judges who die, retire early or are early in their careers, and wrongly assumed all judges eventually reach the target post. On reanalysis, leftist judges are not disadvantaged in the timing of promotion, contrary to Ramseyer and Rasmusen.
refs.factor: Promotion penalty for leftist judges
refs.status: Published critique and reanalysis, a failed replication of a key career-incentive finding.

refs.html: Joan-Josep Vallbé, Carmen Ramírez-Folch (2023). The effect of judges' gender on decisions regarding intimate-partner violence. Journal of Empirical Legal Studies 20(3): 641-668. link
refs.authors: Joan-Josep Vallbé, Carmen Ramírez-Folch
refs.title: The effect of judges' gender on decisions regarding intimate-partner violence
refs.finding: The gender effect is conditional: more experienced female judges are more likely than male colleagues to grant protection orders when caseload is high. A 2021 working-paper version argues that career and promotion dynamics moderate the effects of gender and policy preferences. The authors stress that judges' attributes are unobservable by design in civil-law systems.
refs.jurisdiction: Spain (on-duty pretrial courts, 2010-2018; civil-law career judiciary)
refs.factor: Judge gender x experience x caseload; career incentives

refs.html: Arnaud Philippe (2020). Gender Disparities in Sentencing. Economica 87(348): 1037-1077. link
refs.corrections: Authors, year, venue are correct: Economica 87(348): 1037-1077, DOI 10.1111/ecca.12333. Fix the finding: the 15-day gap is a 33% decrease relative to the 45-day average sentence in the full sample, not 44 days. Corrected finding: Using the universe of French convictions from 2000 to 2003, women received prison sentences about 15 days shorter than comparable men (33% of the 45-day sample mean). The gap also appears in mixed-gender co-offender pairs convicted together on the same day by the same judge for the same crime. The gap depends on judge gender but not prosecutor gender: a one-SD increase in the number of women in the court reduces it by 10%. Drop the blog sentence about paternalistic stereotyping by male judges, or cite the blog separately; it is not in the abstract and could not be verified.
refs.authors: Arnaud Philippe
refs.title: Gender Disparities in Sentencing
refs.finding: Women receive prison terms about 15 days shorter than men (33% of the 44-day mean), even within mixed-gender co-defendant pairs. The gap depends on judge gender but not prosecutor gender: a one-SD increase in women on the bench reduces it by about 10%. The author's blog attributes the gap to protective, paternalistic stereotyping by male judges.
refs.factor: Defendant gender x judge gender

refs.html: Cécile Bourreau-Dubois, Myriam Doriat-Duban, Bruno Jeandidier, Jean-Claude Ray (2020). Does gender diversity in panels of judges matter? Evidence from French child support cases. International Review of Law and Economics 63: 105929. link
refs.authors: Cécile Bourreau-Dubois, Myriam Doriat-Duban, Bruno Jeandidier, Jean-Claude Ray
refs.title: Does gender diversity in panels of judges matter? Evidence from French child support cases
refs.venue: International Review of Law and Economics 63: 105929
refs.finding: Panel gender composition significantly affects child-support amounts. All-female panels set higher amounts than mixed panels regardless of creditor gender, with the gap especially large when the creditor is a man and the panel has two women and one man.
refs.jurisdiction: France (Courts of Appeal; civil-law, highly feminized judiciary)
refs.factor: Gender composition of three-judge panels

refs.html: Raphael Corbi, Rafael Ferreira, Jaqueline Oliveira, Danilo Souza (2021). Female Judges and In-group Bias in Labor Courts. Economics Bulletin (article eb-20-01177). link
refs.authors: Raphael Corbi, Rafael Ferreira, Jaqueline Oliveira, Danilo Souza
refs.title: Female Judges and In-group Bias in Labor Courts
refs.finding: Plaintiffs (workers) are less likely to win before female judges: -1.7 percentage points for male plaintiffs and -2.3 for female plaintiffs. Female judges are harsher on female plaintiffs, the opposite of gender in-group favoritism.
refs.jurisdiction: Brazil (São Paulo labour courts TRT2, 2006-2015; civil-law career judges)
refs.factor: Judge gender x plaintiff gender
refs.status: Published (Economics Bulletin); the authors note mixed prior literature.

refs.html: Guilherme Lambais, Henrik Sigstad (2023). Judicial Subversion: The Effects of Political Power on Court Outcomes. Journal of Public Economics 217: 104788. link
refs.authors: Guilherme Lambais, Henrik Sigstad
refs.title: Judicial Subversion: The Effects of Political Power on Court Outcomes
refs.finding: Candidates who narrowly win local elections are about 60 percentage points more likely than narrow losers to be acquitted in corruption cases filed before the election (an earlier version reported 50 points). The authors attribute this to elected politicians' direct influence over law enforcers rather than better lawyers. In contrast, a separate São Paulo small-claims study (Assumpção & Trecenti, arXiv 2001.00889) finds a 3.7-point penalty against politician litigants.
refs.factor: Litigant political power (identity of the accused) acting on career judges and prosecutors
refs.status: Peer-reviewed. The small-claims contrast shows the effect is context-dependent.

refs.html: Xiqian Cai, Pei Li, Qinyue Luo, Hong Song, Huihua Xie (2025). Do Judges Exhibit Gender Bias? Evidence from the Universe of Divorce Cases in China. ROCKWOOL Foundation Berlin Discussion Paper 23/25. link
refs.authors: Xiqian Cai, Pei Li, Qinyue Luo, Hong Song, Huihua Xie
refs.title: Do Judges Exhibit Gender Bias? Evidence from the Universe of Divorce Cases in China
refs.finding: Female judges are 1.2 percentage points more likely to grant divorce petitions from female than from male plaintiffs, relative to male judges, mainly because they treat male plaintiffs more harshly. The bias is smaller in regions with stronger traditional gender norms, and legal-institutional development has little moderating effect.
refs.factor: Judge gender x plaintiff gender (in-group bias); regional gender norms
refs.status: Working paper (2025), not yet peer-reviewed as far as found.

refs.html: Ernest Liu, Yi Lu, Wenwei Peng, Shaoda Wang (2022). Judicial Independence, Local Protectionism, and Economic Integration: Evidence from China. NBER Working Paper 30432 (2024 draft retitled 'Court Capture, Local Protectionism, and Economic Integration'). link
refs.authors: Ernest Liu, Yi Lu, Wenwei Peng, Shaoda Wang
refs.title: Judicial Independence, Local Protectionism, and Economic Integration: Evidence from China
refs.venue: NBER Working Paper 30432 (2024 draft retitled 'Court Capture, Local Protectionism, and Economic Integration')
refs.finding: Moving courts' finance and personnel control from local to provincial government reduced local defendants' win rate against non-local plaintiffs by 7.0% (7.3% in the 2024 draft), mainly through better decision quality, with stronger effects for politically connected local defendants. Judicial reasoning improved and appeals fell.
refs.factor: Who controls judges' finances and personnel (career incentives / local capture)
refs.status: Working paper; estimates differ by version.

refs.html: John Zhuang Liu, Wenwei Peng, Shaoda Wang, Daniel Xu (2025). The Law and Economics of Lawyers: Evidence from the Revolving Door in China's Judicial System. NBER Working Paper 33708. link
refs.authors: John Zhuang Liu, Wenwei Peng, Shaoda Wang, Daniel Xu
refs.title: The Law and Economics of Lawyers: Evidence from the Revolving Door in China's Judicial System
refs.finding: Former judges turned lawyers ('power lawyers') deliver 8-23% higher win rates for clients. Home-versus-away comparisons suggest both expertise and personal connections matter. These lawyers can improve decisions through evidence and reasoning but also bias them through strategy and connections, so adding more of them has non-monotonic effects on decision quality.
refs.factor: Former-judge lawyers (connections between litigant counsel and sitting judges)

refs.html: Rui Zuo (2025). The Case Assignment System as a Technology: Algorithmic Allocation and Its Impact on Court. Job market paper (University of Texas at Austin / MIT), Sept 15, 2025. link
refs.authors: Rui Zuo
refs.title: The Case Assignment System as a Technology: Algorithmic Allocation and Its Impact on Court
refs.venue: Job market paper (University of Texas at Austin / MIT), Sept 15, 2025
refs.finding: Random assignment reduces path dependence but weakens judge-case expertise matching, with modest performance declines. ML assignment improves matching while maintaining performance. In dangerous-driving cases, both systems increase sentencing variance and leniency.
refs.factor: Case-assignment regime (manual vs random vs ML) and resulting sentencing variance

refs.html: Jakub Drápal, Jose Pina-Sánchez (2023). What is the Value of Judicial Experience? Exploring Judge Trajectories Using Longitudinal Data. Justice Quarterly 40(2): 211-240 (online 2022). link
refs.authors: Jakub Drápal, Jose Pina-Sánchez
refs.title: What is the Value of Judicial Experience? Exploring Judge Trajectories Using Longitudinal Data
refs.finding: More experienced judges impose more prison sentences, use shortened procedures less and convict fewer defendants. Between-judge disparities shrink as judges gain experience, across all outcomes.
refs.factor: Judge experience; between-judge disparity over careers
refs.status: Peer-reviewed; observational (random allocation not confirmed in what was read).

refs.html: Andrzej Uhl, Kamil Mamak (2026). Are sentencing disparities unavoidable? Lessons from centralized judicial training. Journal of Criminal Justice 102: 102582. link
refs.authors: Andrzej Uhl, Kamil Mamak
refs.title: Are sentencing disparities unavoidable? Lessons from centralized judicial training
refs.finding: Despite identical facts and shared centralized training, penalties ranged sixfold (4 to 24 months). Trainees disagreed on which count deserved more, on how to combine penalties, on ancillary orders such as compensation, and on how much to follow the prosecutor's recommendation. The authors conclude that without structured guidelines, judges may continue to impose highly idiosyncratic sentences.
refs.factor: Inter-judge disparity despite common centralized training (training cohort)
refs.status: Peer-reviewed (2026). Earlier Mamak et al. (2022, European Journal of Criminology) found a Polish legislative reform did not radically reduce inter-court disparities.

refs.html: Volker Grundies (2018). Regionale Unterschiede in der gerichtlichen Sanktionspraxis in der Bundesrepublik Deutschland. Eine empirische Analyse. In D. Hermann & A. Pöge (eds.), Kriminalsoziologie, Nomos, pp. 295-316. link
refs.authors: Volker Grundies
refs.title: Regionale Unterschiede in der gerichtlichen Sanktionspraxis in der Bundesrepublik Deutschland. Eine empirische Analyse
refs.venue: In D. Hermann & A. Pöge (eds.), Kriminalsoziologie, Nomos, pp. 295-316
refs.finding: Per secondary citations, sentencing differs considerably across regions and court districts (mainly along a north-south axis) while being relatively homogeneous within districts. Grundies links variation in sentence length to membership of a higher-regional-court (OLG) district, which he explains by the judiciary's hierarchical structure and appellate (Revision) practice.
refs.factor: Inter-court / regional disparity (judge lottery at the court level)
refs.status: Full text not accessed; findings via secondary citation (KriPoZ).

refs.html: The Brussels Times (reporting a CALL/RVV/CCE report) (2020). Asylum seekers more likely to get rejected by Flemish judges (report on Council for Alien Law Litigation statistics 2017-2019). The Brussels Times. link
refs.authors: The Brussels Times (reporting a CALL/RVV/CCE report)
refs.title: Asylum seekers more likely to get rejected by Flemish judges (report on Council for Alien Law Litigation statistics 2017-2019)
refs.finding: Flemish judges rejected 92.4% of asylum appeals and Francophone judges 70.8%. Francophone judges granted 12.18% (805 of 6,608) against 1.2% (90 of 7,530) for Flemish judges. The council president reported no notable language-role difference for visas, family reunification or regularisation, and said harmonisation assemblies had not closed the gap.
refs.factor: Judge group identity (Dutch- vs French-speaking chambers)
refs.status: News report of an official report (the original not opened); the year of the article is inferred from its coverage of 2017-2019 data. A 2024 Hasselt PhD by Diego Vaes on CALL rulings is embargoed until 2029.

refs.html: Nuno Garoupa, Veronica Grembi, Shirley Ching-ping Lin (2011). Explaining Constitutional Review in New Democracies: The Case of Taiwan. Pacific Rim Law & Policy Journal 20(1): 1-40. link
refs.authors: Nuno Garoupa, Veronica Grembi, Shirley Ching-ping Lin
refs.title: Explaining Constitutional Review in New Democracies: The Case of Taiwan
refs.finding: Little support for the attitudinal hypothesis (justices voting with their appointing party). During democratization, justices dissented more and sometimes voted against the dominant party, consistent with building credibility. The follow-up by Dalla Pellegrina, Garoupa & Lin (2012, NTU Law Review 7(1): 123-165), estimating ideal points for 1988-2009, also found no strong appointer-aligned coalitions and mostly moderate justices.
refs.factor: Appointing party (attitudinal hypothesis)

refs.html: Yen-tu Su, Han-wei Ho, Chien-chih Lin (2018). Are Taiwan Constitutional Court Justices Political?. Paper for Comparative Supreme Court Decision Making Workshop, Hebrew University (Dec 2018). link
refs.authors: Yen-tu Su, Han-wei Ho, Chien-chih Lin
refs.title: Are Taiwan Constitutional Court Justices Political?
refs.venue: Paper for Comparative Supreme Court Decision Making Workshop, Hebrew University (Dec 2018)
refs.finding: Contrary to earlier studies, finds circumstantial evidence that political ideology plays some role in Constitutional Court merits decisions, though most justices are ideological moderates. Personality, jurisprudence and judicial philosophy also matter. Argues earlier nulls reflect measurement limits.
refs.factor: Judicial ideology vs judicial philosophy and personality
refs.status: Workshop paper (Academia Sinica authors); peer-reviewed version not confirmed.

refs.html: Kong-Pin Chen, Kuo-Chang Huang, Chang-Ching Lin (2015). Party Capability versus Court Preference: Why Do the 'Haves' Come Out Ahead? An Empirical Lesson from the Taiwan Supreme Court. Journal of Law, Economics, & Organization 31(1): 93-126. link
refs.authors: Kong-Pin Chen, Kuo-Chang Huang, Chang-Ching Lin
refs.title: Party Capability versus Court Preference: Why Do the 'Haves' Come Out Ahead? An Empirical Lesson from the Taiwan Supreme Court
refs.finding: Higher-status litigants had stronger representation and won more, but party capability does not fully explain this. The court's discretionary jurisdiction strongly favoured government litigants at the agenda-setting stage, which the authors link to judges seeing themselves as part of government. A 2015 NTU thesis extending it (Cheng Yu-Hsiang, ~2,000 cases 2008-2009) finds the presiding judge's seniority significantly reduces appeal pass rates, with seniority-by-appellant-type interactions.
refs.factor: Litigant identity (haves vs have-nots, government) and court preference
refs.status: Peer-reviewed. Findings are summarized from the working paper and repository abstracts.

refs.html: Cheng, Yu-Hsiang (2015). Does Court Preference Have an Impact on the Judgement? The Case of the Taiwan Supreme Court. Thesis, Department of Economics, National Taiwan University. link
refs.authors: Cheng, Yu-Hsiang
refs.title: Does Court Preference Have an Impact on the Judgement? The Case of the Taiwan Supreme Court
refs.venue: Thesis, Department of Economics, National Taiwan University
refs.finding: Presiding-judge seniority has a significant negative effect on appeal pass rates, and judges at different seniority levels favour different appellant types differently. The analysis is correlational.
refs.factor: Presiding judge seniority

refs.html: 曾怡鳳 (Yi-Feng Tseng); advisor 陳鎮洲 (2021). 影響法官量刑因素之研究——以槍砲彈藥刀械管制條例為例 (Factors affecting judges' sentencing: the Controlling Guns, Ammunition and Knives Act). Master's thesis, Department of Economics, National Chengchi University. link

refs.venue: Master's thesis, Department of Economics, National Chengchi University
refs.finding: Judge gender and region significantly affect sentencing: male judges' prison terms average about 1.3 months longer than female judges', and courts in special municipalities sentence about 1.4 months shorter. The analysis is correlational.
refs.factor: Judge gender, gender ratio, court region

refs.html: 余一鳴, 邱保龍, 吳永明, 陳昆皇 (Yi-Ming Yu, Pao-Lung Chiu, Yung-Ming Wu, Kun-Huang Chen) (2023). 貪污審判存在性別差異嗎？2011-2020年地方法院裁判書的文字探勘 (Do Corruption Trials Feature a Gender Difference? Text Mining of District Court Verdicts, 2011-2020). Journal of Public Administration (公共行政學報) 64: 1-33. link
refs.authors: 余一鳴, 邱保龍, 吳永明, 陳昆皇 (Yi-Ming Yu, Pao-Lung Chiu, Yung-Ming Wu, Kun-Huang Chen)
refs.title: 貪污審判存在性別差異嗎？2011-2020年地方法院裁判書的文字探勘 (Do Corruption Trials Feature a Gender Difference? Text Mining of District Court Verdicts, 2011-2020)
refs.venue: Journal of Public Administration (公共行政學報) 64: 1-33
